cases.title: Word-list recall in older adults at three delays
cases.context: Researchers interested in how memory fades in older adults did a study to evaluate delayed recall (the number of words a person can repeat back from a list heard earlier). Five adults aged 70 to 79 years heard a list of 15 unrelated words. Each subject was asked to recall the list immediately, again after 20 minutes and again after 24 hours. The table below shows the number of words recalled (words) at each delay. Assume that any quantities of interest are Normally distributed.
tasks: Is there a difference in the number of words recalled over time? DO NOT use R. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Use a significance level of \(\alpha=0.05\) for your inference. (Note: If a difference exists, do not identify which delays are different.)

hypotheses.alternative: H_A:\text{not all three population means are equal}
hypotheses.nullWords: The mean number of words recalled by older adults is the same immediately, after 20 minutes and after 24 hours.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The mean number of words recalled differs for at least one of the three delays.

cases.symbols: \(x_{ts}\) (observation for treatment \(t\), subject \(s\)), \(m\) (number of treatments), \(n\) (number of subjects), \(\bar S_s\) (subject mean), \(\bar T_t\) (treatment mean), \(\bar X\) (grand mean), \(SS\) (sum of squares), \(DF\) (degrees of freedom), \(MS\) (mean square), \(F\) (F statistic).

steps.title: State the procedure and design
steps.words: The same 5 adults are tested at all 3 delays, so the observations are repeated measures on the same subjects. The procedure is repeated measures ANOVA. It removes the large differences between people from the error term before comparing the delays.

steps.title: State the hypotheses
steps.words: The mean number of words recalled by older adults is the same immediately, after 20 minutes and after 24 hours. The mean number of words recalled differs for at least one of the three delays.

steps.title: Calculate each subject mean
steps.words: Average each subject across all 3 treatments. Each row of the table gives one subject mean.

steps.title: Calculate the treatment means and the grand mean
steps.words: Average each column over the 5 subjects. The grand mean is the mean of all 15 observations, which equals the mean of the treatment means.

steps.title: Calculate the within-subjects sum of squares
steps.words: Each subject is compared only with its own mean, so differences between subjects never enter this sum. It holds the treatment effect plus residual scatter.

steps.title: Calculate the treatment sum of squares
steps.words: Multiply by n because each treatment mean involves n subjects.

steps.title: Calculate the residual sum of squares
steps.words: The residual is the within-subject variation that the treatment means do not explain.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom and mean squares
steps.words: Each sum of squares is divided by its own degrees of freedom to give a variance estimate.

steps.title: Calculate the F statistic
steps.words: Treatment variance is compared with residual variance. Values near 1 or below are what equal treatment means produce.

steps.title: Find the critical value
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open F_table.pdf, PDF page 1. Use numerator column ν_n=2 and denominator row ν_d=8. The lightface entry 4.46 is the 0.05 cutoff and the boldface entry 8.65 is the 0.01 cutoff. Swapping the two df selects a different, wrong cell.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: F is above both the 0.05 and the 0.01 cutoffs, so reject the null hypothesis with P < 0.01.

cases.conclusion: F = 46.968 with 2 and 8 degrees of freedom exceeds F_0.01(2,8) = 8.65. Reject H0, P < 0.01. There is a difference in the mean number of words recalled over time. Holm-corrected pairwise t tests are then needed to locate which delays differ.

cases.title: Holm comparisons of the three recall delays
cases.context: In a study of word-list recall, 5 older adults were each asked to recall a list of 15 words immediately, again after 20 minutes and again after 24 hours. A repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed on the data, resulting in the conclusion that there is a difference in the number of words recalled among the three delays (F = 46.968 with 2 and 8 degrees of freedom, P < 0.01). From the ANOVA, the mean number of words recalled was 10 immediately, 8 after 20 minutes and 5.6 after 24 hours. The residual mean square was \(MS_{res}=0.516667\) with \(DF_{res}=8\) and n = 5 subjects.
tasks: Perform the appropriate form of multiple pairwise comparisons, testing every delay against every other delay, using the Holm correction to determine which of the three delays differ from one another. Use the relevant information from the ANOVA results given above to do your calculations.

Present your final/overall conclusion on which delays are different from one another (and which delays are not different) using an overall level of significance of 0.05. Please state how you reached your conclusions.

hypotheses.nullWords: For the pair being compared, mean number of words recalled is the same at the two delays.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: For that pair, mean number of words recalled differs between the two delays.

cases.symbols: \(\bar T_i\) (treatment mean), \(MS_{res}\) (residual mean square), \(n\) (number of subjects), \(DF_{res}\) (residual degrees of freedom), \(k\) (number of pairwise comparisons), \(\alpha_j\) (Holm level for the \(j\)th comparison), \(\alpha_T\) (overall level).

steps.title: State the procedure
steps.words: The overall F test rejected, so pairwise t tests locate the differences. The repeated-measures version uses MS_res in the standard error and DF_res for the t table.

steps.title: State the hypotheses for each pair
steps.words: For the pair being compared, mean number of words recalled is the same at the two delays. For that pair, mean number of words recalled differs between the two delays.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of a difference
steps.words: The same standard error serves every pair because every treatment mean is based on the same n subjects.

steps.title: Calculate every pairwise t statistic
steps.words: Keep the subtraction order. The sign only gives the direction, and the ranking uses |t|.

steps.title: Order by |t| and set the Holm levels
steps.words: The largest |t| is tested at the strictest level. Testing stops at the first comparison that is not significant.

steps.title: Comparison 1: Immediate vs 24 hours
steps.words: The 0.0167 column is not printed. In t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 8, the printed neighbors are the 0.02 column (2.896) and the 0.01 column (3.355). Use the stricter 0.01 column, 3.355, because a statistic beyond it is significant at 0.0167 as well. |t| = 9.679 > 3.355, so the Immediate and 24 hours means differ (P < 0.001 before adjustment).

steps.title: Comparison 2: 20 minutes vs 24 hours
steps.words: The 0.025 column is not printed. In t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 8, the printed neighbors are the 0.05 column (2.306) and the 0.02 column (2.896). Use the stricter 0.02 column, 2.896, because a statistic beyond it is significant at 0.025 as well. |t| = 5.279 > 2.896, so the 20 minutes and 24 hours means differ (P < 0.001 before adjustment).

steps.title: Comparison 3: Immediate vs 20 minutes
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 8, combined two-tail 0.05 column, which gives 2.306. |t| = 4.399 > 2.306, so the Immediate and 20 minutes means differ (0.002 < P < 0.005 before adjustment).

cases.conclusion: All three pairs of delays differ at the Holm-corrected levels. Fewer words are recalled after 20 minutes than immediately, and fewer again after 24 hours. For Immediate vs 24 hours, t = 9.679. For 20 minutes vs 24 hours, t = 5.279. For Immediate vs 20 minutes, t = 4.399.

Assume that any quantities of interest are Normally distributed.
tasks: Is there a difference in motion coherence threshold under the three conditions? DO NOT use R. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.

steps.title: Make the decision

cases.title: Stuttering before and after fluency shaping therapy
cases.context: In a clinical trial, 38 adults referred to a speech clinic for stuttering (speech broken by repeated sounds, stretched sounds and blocks) were examined before and again three months after starting fluency shaping therapy (practice in slow speech with a gentle start to each phrase). At each visit a speech-language pathologist (a clinician who assesses and treats speech disorders) recorded whether stuttering was present or absent while the patient read a passage aloud. The table below shows the number of patients with each pair of results.
tasks: Based on the recorded data, is there evidence that the presence of stuttering is different before and after fluency shaping therapy? DO NOT use R.
Use a significance level of \(\alpha=0.05\) for your inference and apply the Yates correction (the continuity correction for a 2 x 2 table). Please state how you reached your conclusions.

hypotheses.nullWords: Fluency shaping therapy has no effect on the presence of stuttering, so a patient whose result changes is equally likely to change from present to absent as from absent to present.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The two directions of change are not equally likely, so the presence of stuttering differs before and after the therapy.

cases.symbols: \(a,d\) (subjects with the same result both times), \(b,c\) (subjects whose result changes), \(E\) (expected number in each change cell), \(\chi^2\) (McNemar chi-square), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: State the procedure
steps.words: Each patient is classified twice, before and after the therapy, so the two classifications are paired nominal data. This design is the nominal version of the paired t test, and the procedure is McNemar's test.

steps.title: State the hypotheses
steps.words: Fluency shaping therapy has no effect on the presence of stuttering, so a patient whose result changes is equally likely to change from present to absent as from absent to present. The two directions of change are not equally likely, so the presence of stuttering differs before and after the therapy.

steps.title: Show why the independent chi-square is wrong here
steps.words: Treating the before and after results as two independent samples gives chi-square = 0.38, which would wrongly suggest no change. The rows and columns describe the same patients, so they are not independent and this test is not valid for the design.

steps.title: Identify the subjects who change
steps.words: Only discordant subjects carry information about a change. Here b counts patients with stuttering present before and absent after and c counts patients with stuttering absent before and present after. The concordant cells a = 12 and d = 8 do not enter the statistic.

steps.title: Calculate the expected number in each change cell
steps.words: If the null hypothesis is true, the changes split evenly in the two directions.

steps.title: Calculate the McNemar chi-square with Yates correction
steps.words: Subtract one half from each absolute difference before squaring because the table is 2 x 2 (Yates correction).

steps.title: Find the critical value
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open Chi_Squared_Table2.pdf, PDF page 1. Row df = 1, column χ².050 gives 3.841. The same row gives 2.706 in the .100 column, 5.024 in the .025 column, 6.635 in the .010 column and 7.879 in the .005 column for a P range.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: Reject the null hypothesis because the statistic is above the cutoff. The P range is 0.005<P<0.01.

cases.conclusion: McNemar chi-square = 6.722 with 1 df exceeds chi-square_0.05(1) = 3.841 and chi-square_0.01(1) = 6.635 but not chi-square_0.005(1) = 7.879. Reject H0, 0.005 < P < 0.01. There is a difference in the presence of stuttering before and after fluency shaping therapy. Of the 18 patients who changed, 15 went from present to absent and 3 went from absent to present.

cases.title: Computerized memory screening test against a neuropsychologist
cases.context: In a study looking at screening for dementia, 36 patients referred to a memory clinic were each assessed by two methods. A five-minute computerized screening test classified each patient as impaired or not impaired. A neuropsychologist (a clinician who gives a full set of memory and thinking tests) made the same classification without seeing the screening result. The table below shows the number of patients with each pair of classifications.
tasks: Based on the recorded data, is there evidence that the proportion of patients classified as impaired is different for the two methods? Use a chi-square test. DO NOT use R.
Use a significance level of \(\alpha=0.05\) for your inference and apply the Yates correction (the continuity correction for a 2 x 2 table). Please state how you reached your conclusions.

hypotheses.nullWords: There is no difference between the screening test and the neuropsychologist in how often a patient is classified as impaired, so disagreements are equally likely in either direction.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The two methods differ in how often they classify a patient as impaired.

cases.symbols: \(a,d\) (subjects with the same result both times), \(b,c\) (subjects whose result changes), \(E\) (expected number in each change cell), \(\chi^2\) (McNemar chi-square), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: State the procedure
steps.words: Both methods classify the same 36 patients, so the results are paired nominal data. The procedure is McNemar's test, which compares two diagnostic procedures applied to the same people.

steps.title: State the hypotheses
steps.words: There is no difference between the screening test and the neuropsychologist in how often a patient is classified as impaired, so disagreements are equally likely in either direction. The two methods differ in how often they classify a patient as impaired.

steps.title: Identify the subjects who change
steps.words: Only discordant subjects carry information about a change. Here b counts patients called impaired by the screening test but not by the neuropsychologist and c counts patients called impaired by the neuropsychologist but not by the screening test. The concordant cells a = 11 and d = 8 do not enter the statistic.

steps.title: Calculate the expected number in each change cell
steps.words: If the null hypothesis is true, the changes split evenly in the two directions.

steps.title: Calculate the McNemar chi-square with Yates correction
steps.words: Subtract one half from each absolute difference before squaring because the table is 2 x 2 (Yates correction).

steps.title: Find the critical value
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open Chi_Squared_Table2.pdf, PDF page 1. Row df = 1, column χ².050 gives 3.841. The same row gives 2.706 in the .100 column, 5.024 in the .025 column, 6.635 in the .010 column and 7.879 in the .005 column for a P range.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: Do not reject the null hypothesis because the statistic is below the cutoff. The P range is 0.05<P<0.10.

cases.conclusion: McNemar chi-square = 3.765 with 1 df is slightly below chi-square_0.05(1) = 3.841 and above chi-square_0.10(1) = 2.706. Do not reject H0 (0.05 < P < 0.10). There is no evidence of a difference between the screening test and the neuropsychologist in the proportion of patients classified as impaired, even though the screening test alone calls 13 patients impaired and the neuropsychologist alone calls 4. The result is close to the cutoff, so a larger study could settle the question.

cases.title: Acoustic voice analysis program against a speech-language pathologist
cases.context: The table below shows data on 40 voice recordings from a voice clinic. In each recording a patient held the vowel "ah" for 5 seconds. Each recording was classified as hoarse or not hoarse by an acoustic analysis program (software that measures how irregular the vibration of the vocal folds is from one cycle to the next). The same recordings were classified by a clinician (a speech-language pathologist, who assesses and treats voice and speech disorders) who listened to each recording and did not see the output of the program.
tasks: Based on the recorded data, is there evidence that the proportion of recordings classified as hoarse is different for the two methods? Use a chi-square test. DO NOT use R.
Use a significance level of \(\alpha=0.05\) for your inference and apply the Yates correction (the continuity correction for a 2 x 2 table). Please state how you reached your conclusions.

steps.words: Only discordant subjects carry information about a change. Here b counts recordings called hoarse by the program but not by the clinician and c counts recordings called hoarse by the clinician but not by the program. The concordant cells a = 12 and d = 13 do not enter the statistic.

steps.title: Find the critical value
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open Chi_Squared_Table2.pdf, PDF page 1. Row df = 1, column χ².050 gives 3.841. The same row gives 2.706 in the .100 column, 5.024 in the .025 column, 6.635 in the .010 column and 7.879 in the .005 column for a P range.

steps.words: Reject the null hypothesis because the statistic is above the cutoff. The P range is P<0.005.

cases.conclusion: McNemar chi-square = 9.6 with 1 df exceeds chi-square_0.005(1) = 7.879. Reject H0, P < 0.005. There is a difference between the two methods. questions.stem: In the study of word-list recall in 5 older adults, the treatment means are 10, 8 and 5.6 words (immediate, 20 minutes, 24 hours) and the grand mean is 7.8667 words. What is \(SS_{treat}\)?
questions.why: Multiply the sum of squared deviations of the treatment means (9.7067) by n = 5. Leaving out n gives 9.7067, 52.6667 is the within-subjects sum of squares and 24.2667 is the mean square.

questions.stem: In the reach error study (6 volunteers, 3 practice blocks), \(SS_{treat}=562.3333\) and \(SS_{res}=59\). What is the repeated-measures F statistic?
questions.why: MS_treat = 562.3333/2 and MS_res = 59/10, so F = 47.655. Dividing SS_res by 12 uses the within-subjects df, and 9.531 is the ratio of the sums of squares without their df.

questions.stem: Contrast sensitivity is measured in the same 5 subjects under dim, medium and bright room lighting. Why is a repeated-measures ANOVA used here and not a one-way ANOVA?
options: Because there are only 5 subjects, and a one-way ANOVA needs at least 10 per group
Because the same subjects are measured under all three conditions, so differences between subjects can be removed from the error term
Because contrast sensitivity is a nominal variable
Because three conditions always require a Holm correction before any F test
questions.why: A one-way ANOVA assumes three independent groups. Here every subject gives three values, so the test uses the residual left after the subject differences are taken out.

questions.stem: After the reach error ANOVA (n = 6, \(MS_{res}=5.9\), \(DF_{res}=10\)), what is the standard error of a difference between two block means?
questions.why: SE = sqrt(2 MS_res/n) with n = 6 subjects. Leaving out the 2 gives 0.99163, forgetting the square root gives 1.9667, and dividing by DF_res instead of n gives 1.0863.

questions.stem: A repeated-measures ANOVA on pupil diameter under three levels of mental load rejects equal means. Three pairwise t tests follow with the Holm correction and \(\alpha_T=0.05\). At what level is the comparison with the largest \(|t|\) tested?
questions.why: With k = 3 comparisons the first Holm level is 0.05/(3 - 1 + 1) = 0.0167. The next two comparisons are tested at 0.025 and 0.05, and testing stops at the first one that is not significant.

questions.stem: In the stuttering study, 15 patients changed from stuttering present to stuttering absent after the therapy and 3 changed from absent to present (12 stayed present, 8 stayed absent). What is the McNemar chi-square with the Yates correction?
questions.why: E = (15 + 3)/2 = 9 and each term is (6 - 0.5)^2/9 = 3.361, so chi-square = 6.722. Leaving out the one half gives 8, and 0.38 is the independent-samples chi-square, which ignores the pairing.

questions.stem: In the phantom limb pain study of 28 amputees, 6 had pain both times, 15 changed from pain to no pain, 5 changed from no pain to pain and 2 had no pain both times. What is the expected number E in each change cell?
questions.why: Only the 20 subjects who changed are used, and under the null hypothesis they split evenly, so E = (15 + 5)/2 = 10. Dividing all 28 subjects by 4 gives 7 and by 2 gives 14, and both wrongly include the subjects who did not change.

questions.stem: Thirty patients are classified as having a migraine aura or not in the month before and the month after starting a preventive drug. Which patients enter the McNemar chi-square?
options: Only the patients with an aura in both months
All 30 patients, through the row and column totals
Only the patients with an aura in the first month
Only the patients whose classification changes between the two months
questions.why: The statistic uses the two discordant cells b and c. Patients with the same result both times say nothing about the direction of change.

questions.stem: In the memory clinic study, 13 patients were called impaired by the screening test only and 4 by the neuropsychologist only. What is the McNemar chi-square with the Yates correction, and what is the decision at \(\alpha=0.05\)?
questions.why: E = 8.5 and each term is (4.5 - 0.5)^2/8.5 = 1.882, so chi-square = 3.765, which is below 3.841. Leaving out the Yates correction gives 4.765 and a wrong rejection.

questions.stem: Two radiologists each read the same 35 brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and classify each scan as lesion or no lesion. Which procedure tests whether the two readers differ in how often they report a lesion?
options: A chi-square test of independence on the 2 x 2 table of all 35 scans
An unpaired t test on the two readers
McNemar's test on the scans where the two readers disagree
A repeated-measures ANOVA with two conditions
questions.why: Both readers classify the same scans, so the two sets of nominal results are paired. The ordinary chi-square test assumes independent samples and is not valid for this design.

notes: All data are invented for practice. Sources of printed critical values are F_table.pdf (rows 6, 8, 10, column 2), t_table.pdf page 1 (rows 8 and 10) and Chi_Squared_Table2.pdf (row df = 1).

Holm levels 0.0167 and 0.025 are not printed columns of the t table, so each is replaced by the next stricter printed column (0.01 and 0.02), as in the reference cases. No t statistic falls between the bracketing columns, so the decisions do not depend on this choice.

n21-b-motion-coherence-colour (repeated measures) and n21-b-neglect-prism and n21-b-memory-screen-neuropsych (McNemar) do not reject. n21-b-memory-screen-neuropsych (3.765) and n21-b-phantom-pain-mirror (4.05) are close to the 3.841 cutoff on either side.

The spec forbids colons and semicolons in tasks, words, context and conclusion, so the reference wording that used them was rephrased. Step titles of the form 'Comparison 1: A vs B' are kept exactly as in the reference Holm cases.
values.exactP is stored (same key as the reference cases) but no exact P is quoted in any solution text. Only printed-table P ranges are used.

The three s21mcnemar cases carry the extra step 'Show why the independent chi-square is wrong here' and the values keys independentChi2 and independentExpected, as in the reference p7 case. The two s21diagnostic cases follow the 7-step reference diagnostic case.
The two Holm cases reuse the unrounded treatment means and MS_res of their parent ANOVA case in values. The work lines show them rounded.
